title: Module 5 practice assessment
description: Ungraded practice for Module 5. Take it as often as you like, and read the feedback after each question; it points back to the lesson section that explains the answer.

questions.prompt: A recovered GDD says the player shoots with F9 and tags the claim `[OBSERVED]`. `project.godot` stores the binding as the integer 4194326. What is the right way to settle whether the tag is correct?
choices: Open the cited line in `project.godot` and check that the line number points at the shoot binding; once the line is confirmed, the tag's key name needs no further check.
Ask Godot what the stored integer means, for example with a one-line `SceneTree` script that prints `OS.get_keycode_string(4194326)`, and compare the printed name with F9.
Re-run the reverse pass with Zelda's questions and gates switched on, and keep F9 if the second pass, run on the same source files, reproduces the same claim and tag.
Check that `IMPLEMENTATION-MAP.md` and the GDD's input section both give F9; two documents from one recovered design agreeing is enough to keep the tag.
questions.feedback: A tag is a claim about evidence, not evidence, and `project.godot` stores keys as integers, so only asking Godot decodes 4194326: it prints `Ctrl`, while `KEY_F9` is 4194340. A correct line number, a second pass and a second document from the same run all repeat the agent's claim without checking it. See "Provenance tags" and the audit list in Build It.

questions.prompt: Public Walker `main` does not contain the `gdd/` folder. What does the public repository offer for the GDD step, and what are its limits?
choices: `prompts/zelda-gdd.md`, which becomes a working `/gdd` command with `draft` and `status` once it is copied into `.claude/skills`, though `reverse` is still missing.

The public `publish.sh`, which installs the `gdd` skill when run with `--engine godot --agent claude`, after which `render_dir.py` fills in the skill's tokens and a `CLAUDE.md` is written for the project.
Nothing for the GDD step itself: public `main` only installs `asset-gen`, so without the instructor's local copy the audit cannot be practised on any GDD.
`prompts/zelda-gdd.md`, which can be handed to an agent as plain instructions but installs no `/gdd` command and has no `reverse` spec, so the audit uses an existing GDD.
questions.feedback: The public repository carries the reusable prompt `prompts/zelda-gdd.md` but not the skill, so there is no `/gdd` command and no `reverse` spec; its `publish.sh` installs only `asset-gen`. The audit can still be practised on a GDD that already exists. See "Do you have /gdd?" in the Walker example and Route 2 in Build It.

questions.prompt: Which version of this checkpoint criterion could a stranger turn into a test without asking you anything, including where the respawn point is?
choices: After activation, holding `reset_position` for 5 frames at `--fixed-fps 60` leaves the player within 0.2 m of a `Marker3D` child of the pad that sits no more than 0.2 m above the pad's top surface.

After activation, holding `reset_position` for 5 frames at `--fixed-fps 60` leaves the player within 0.2 m of the pad's respawn point, taken from the value the pad's script computes when the player enters.

After activation, the player is within 0.2 m of a `Marker3D` child of the pad, which sits no more than 0.2 m above the pad's top surface, 0.1 s of real time after `reset_position` is pressed, on whatever machine runs the test.
After activation, holding `reset_position` for 5 frames at `--fixed-fps 60` puts the player at a `Marker3D` child of the pad that sits no more than 0.2 m above the pad's top surface.
questions.feedback: A stranger can test a criterion only if it names the quantity and unit, a tolerance, a time box in the engine's clock, how the state is reached, and what the distance is measured against. Each wrong choice drops one of those; measuring against a respawn point the pad computes for itself is the gap in the example's criterion 4, and naming a `Marker3D` child closes it. See "Acceptance criteria a machine can check" and the third item under "What the agents got wrong".

questions.prompt: Criterion 5 of the checkpoint pad sets the player's position below y = -12 directly and checks that the player returns to the respawn point. What does a pass establish?
choices: That a player who walks off an edge during normal play is returned to the pad, because the test reproduces the same fall a player would make.
That the respawn point is a sensible place, just above the pad's surface, because the player has to land within 0.2 m of it for the check to pass.
That the fall branch of the reset code sends the player to the respawn point in headless play, though not that a player can actually reach that state.
That a player who has just respawned can see the pad and tell why they reappeared there, since the check ends with the player standing at the respawn point.
questions.feedback: A constructed fixture and an input-driven check prove different things, and both are legitimate when the criterion says which is which. Criterion 5 tests the fall branch of the code, not a fall a player makes, and it measures against a respawn point the pad computes for itself, so it says nothing about where that point sits or whether anyone can see the pad. See "Acceptance criteria a machine can check", Predict question 3 and the third item under "What the agents got wrong".

questions.prompt: Which sentence is an honest scoping line for the OpenXR build (`walker-xr-openxr-character-centric-movement`) in a GDD's technical section?
choices: It was verified only by import; OpenXR initialization fails without a headset, so everything that needs a headset is unverified, and nothing beyond a clean import is claimed.
It is verified in simulation: arrow keys move the origin and the native mobile XR interface initializes, so only stereo pixels and head tracking remain unverified.
It is supported, because the project imports cleanly and the headless run exited with code 0 without errors; only how good it looks in a headset is left unverified.
It is expected to work on standalone headsets, because the project imports cleanly and Godot recommends the Mobile renderer for them; only desktop VR is left unverified.
questions.feedback: An honest scoping sentence is a requirement, a verified fact or a named unverified item. This build's record is import only: OpenXR initialization fails when no headset is detected. Arrow-key movement belongs to the mobile VR build, and a clean import, exit code 0 or a renderer recommendation is not hardware evidence. See "Scoping mobile, networked, and XR worlds".

questions.prompt: Codex finished the checkpoint pad and said the partial test's criterion-1 check "was raycasting against the pad itself." What did the audit show?
choices: Codex was right: the ray hit the pad's `Area3D` itself, so the old check was a false positive, which Codex removed by rewriting criterion 1 around the pad's bottom face.
Codex was half right: a ray hits areas by default, and the old check reached the pad only because `collide_with_areas` had been left on, which Codex's rewrite switched off.
The ray started inside the player body and hit it rather than the pad or the floor, which is why the old check passed when it should have failed.
By default a ray ignores areas: it hit the GridMap floor at y = -6.0 and hit the pad only with `collide_with_areas = true`, so the old check was weak for another reason.
questions.feedback: The second agent improved the test but misdescribed the bug: a ray ignores areas unless `collide_with_areas` is true, so it was never hitting the pad's `Area3D`, and the old check was weak for a different reason. That is why you check an agent's explanation as well as its result; the example record keeps the audit script and its log. See "What the agents got wrong".
